newsitem.title: UK: Hanson counts down to demerger as era ends.
newsitem.headline: Hanson counts down to demerger as era ends.

text.p: Britain's once mighty conglomerate Hanson Plc marks the end of an era next week, capping decades of wheeler-dealing with the flotation of the first two businesses under a four-way demerger.

Shareholders "overwhelmingly" approved the plans on Wednesday -- clearing the decks for Imperial Tobacco to start trading on the London Stock Exchange on October 1. Millennium Chemicals kicks off dealings the day after in New York.

Lord Hanson, the takeover king of British industry, marked the occasion this week by announcing he would step down as chairman of the group on September 30 1997, having steered the industrial combine for more than three decades.
Hanson will float off the Energy Group early in 1997, with the chairman remaining as the patriarch of the rump building group which retains the family name.
Lord Hanson told shareholders at the extraordinary general meeting "All these four grandchildren of mine are going to do extremely well when they are on their own."
But just days before the first demerger, the group was hit by news of a group legal action against Imperial Tobacco in the British courts by cancer victims.
The court action is seen as an eleventh hour blow for Hanson, whose Imperial unit had until now remained untainted by the threat of litigation.

"This has to be factored into the Imperial Tobacco valuation," SBC Warburg analyst Mark Duffy said. "Maybe the share's yield premium should be 50 percent rather than the 40 percent (initially considered right)," he added.

Litigation was one of many factors, together with asset writedowns in the coal and aggregates unit, which have dogged the Hanson shareprice in the run-up to the split. This week it hit a 150 pence low from its 283 pence peak in 1993.
Hanson closed flat on Friday at 154 1/2 pence, with a huge volume of 47 and a half million shares traded by 1600 GMT.

The group's breakup value had been pitched at 150 pence to 200 pence per share, before the latest Imperial news. It will float companies with a capitalisation of more than two billion pounds ($3.12 billion) apiece, according to estimates.
That is a far cry from the humble beginnings when 1950s playboys Hanson and his partner the late Lord White started out.
Hanson began in 1950 as a Yorkshire based fertiliser supplier and was built into a worldwide sprawling corporate giant with annual sales of 11 billion pounds.

Its trailblazing philosophy of mounting hostile takeovers of sickly underperformers and returning them to health widened the Hanson empire to embrace businesses from coal and power supply to tobacco and construction. It also spawned a legion of imitators.

But the fashion for conglomerate stocks has now passed, epitomised by Hanson's breakup decision in January as it began to find it more difficult to squeeze value out of companies with limited growth potential within the group.
Hanson told shareholders this week: "The business did get so big that it was unable to receive a shot in the arm from big acquisitions."

One analyst said: "Traditionally Hanson's profit growth came from slashing costs rather than raising sales. Its managers were steeped in the theory of cost control. So the challenge now facing the demerged companies is -- inject fresh blood to tackle sales." ($1=.6405 Pound)
